title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes and no, thank, apologise and say goodbye in Kannada.
intro:
Kannada greetings are warm and practical. ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ *namaskāra* works with anyone at any time of day, usually with palms joined. Among friends, people skip formal greetings and ask ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀಯ? 'how are you?' or even ಊಟ ಆಯ್ತಾ? 'have you eaten?'.

In this unit you'll also meet the two words for 'you': polite ನೀವು *nīvu* and informal ನೀನು *nīnu*. Remember from the start: vocabulary lists give the neutral standard form; phrases give what people actually say in Bengaluru and Mysuru.

vocab.note: The all-purpose respectful greeting. Plural ನಮಸ್ಕಾರಗಳು is even more formal.
Spoken also ಹೂಂ hūṃ 'yeah'. ಹೌದಾ? haudā? = 'really?'
Denies identity: ಇದು ಕಾಫಿ ಅಲ್ಲ 'this is not coffee'.
More formal: ಧನ್ಯವಾದಗಳು. Everyday speech often uses English ಥ್ಯಾಂಕ್ಸ್ thyāṅks.
Rather formal; politeness is more often shown with the polite verb form (ಕೊಡಿ, ಹೇಳಿ).

vocab.en: it's okay, never mind; not bad

vocab.note: ಆರಾಮಾ? ārāmā? 'all well?' is a very common greeting.
Only for friends, children, younger family. Can be rude to strangers.
Polite imperative of ಬರು 'come'. Informal: ಬಾ bā.
Used on radio, in schools and messages; in daily life people just say ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ.
Also a conversation opener: ಮತ್ತೆ? 'So, what's new?'
Used to any man in a service or formal context. For women: ಮೇಡಂ mēḍam, or ಅಮ್ಮ amma for older women.

phrases.note: Reply: ಆರಾಮ, ನೀವು? or ಹೂಂ, ಆರಾಮ.

phrases.en: Goodbye (lit. go and come back), said by the host
phrases.note: Kannadigas avoid saying just 'go'. The person leaving says ಹೋಗಿ ಬರ್ತೀನಿ hōgi bartīni 'I'll go and come back'.

phrases.en: Bye, I'm off (lit. I'll go and come back)
Please say it a bit slowly

grammar.title: Word order: subject – object – verb
grammar.body:
Kannada puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence. The usual order is subject – (time) – (place) – object – verb. English 'I drink coffee' becomes 'I coffee drink': ನಾನು ಕಾಫಿ ಕುಡಿಯುತ್ತೇನೆ.

Question words don't move to the front: they sit where the answer would be. 'Your name what?' = ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹೆಸರು ಏನು?

A yes/no question just adds **-ಆ** *-ā* to the last word: ಆರಾಮ 'fine' → ಆರಾಮಾ? 'fine?'. Words can be dropped when obvious, especially the subject, because the verb ending already tells you who is doing it.

examples.en: What is your name? (lit. your name what?)

grammar.title: Polite ನೀವು vs informal ನೀನು, and written vs spoken
grammar.body:
Kannada has two words for 'you'. **ನೀವು** *nīvu* is polite and also plural: use it with strangers, elders, shopkeepers, teachers, in-laws. **ನೀನು** *nīnu* is for close friends, younger siblings and children; using it with a stranger sounds rude.

The verb changes with the pronoun, so politeness shows even when the pronoun is dropped: ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ? (polite) vs ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀಯ? (informal); ಬನ್ನಿ 'come' (polite) vs ಬಾ (informal).

**Written vs spoken.** Standard written Kannada uses long verb endings (ಇದ್ದೇನೆ, ಇದ್ದೀರಿ); everyday Bengaluru/Mysuru speech shortens them (ಇದ್ದೀನಿ, ಇದ್ದೀರ). Both are 'correct': use spoken forms in conversation and expect written forms in signs, news and books. Other regions have their own colloquial forms (North Karnataka: ಐತೆ for ಇದೆ), which you'll understand with time.

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Anita meets her elderly neighbour, Mr. Rao, outside their apartment building in Bengaluru one morning.

lines.speaker: Anita
lines.en: I'm fine, sir. How are you?

lines.speaker: Anita
lines.native: ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ ಸಾರ್, ಆಫೀಸಿಗೆ ತಡ ಆಯ್ತು. ಹೋಗಿ ಬರ್ತೀನಿ.
lines.roman: kṣamisi sār, āphīsige taḍa āytu. hōgi bartīni.
lines.en: Sorry sir, I'm late for the office. I'll be off.

culture: Kannadigas rarely say a bare 'goodbye'. The leaver says ಹೋಗಿ ಬರ್ತೀನಿ 'I'll go and come back' and the host answers ಹೋಗಿ ಬನ್ನಿ 'go and come back'. Older women are often addressed as ಅಮ್ಮ 'mother', and young women by elders as ಅಮ್ಮ too, affectionately. Men are ಸಾರ್ in shops and offices, and ಅಣ್ಣ 'elder brother' or ಗುರು 'guru' among young Bengalureans (ಏನ್ ಗುರು? 'what's up, man?').
